title: 94 Meetings

jokes.text: Ben asks for advice about asking Ann to move in, then interrupts the advisor mid-sentence with 'I intend to marry her.'
jokes.setup: Ben presents himself as genuinely uncertain, asking 'Good idea? Bad idea? You tell me?' — framing it as an open question needing guidance.
jokes.punchline: Before the advisor can even finish cautioning that some women need marriage on the horizon, Ben cuts them off: 'I intend to marry her.' He already knew his answer.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the character performs uncertainty he doesn't actually have. Works because it instantly establishes Ben's earnest, hyper-prepared personality. The interruption timing is key structural comedy: he cuts off the caveat because the caveat doesn't apply.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Realskies.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'For realskies? I'm not really quite sure how I feel. I'm happy for them. They're my friends. It makes me a little nauseous. If I could just sum it up in one word, it would be, um...'
jokes.setup: Leslie is asked to react to Ben's plan to propose to Ann. She tries to be positive — 'I'm happy for them' — but her visible discomfort undercuts it completely.
jokes.punchline: She trails off trying to find 'one word' to summarize, setting up the wordless gasp that follows.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's deeply character-specific to Leslie — her relentless positivity crashing against genuine feeling. The escalating contradiction ('happy for them...nauseous') is well-structured, and trailing off into silence is the right instinct, setting up the gasp punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need one word to sum up my feelings about Andy and Ann... *makes extended uncomfortable sound*

jokes.text: [gasps] Ohhhhhhhhhhhh.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been fumbling for one word to describe how she feels about Ann and Ben's future marriage.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a word, she just gasps and lets out a prolonged, overwhelmed 'Ohhhhhh' — the emotion is too big for language.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic economy. The buildup asks for 'one word' and the payoff is zero words — just raw, unprocessed feeling. Amy Poehler's physicality is implied by the transcript and the joke lives entirely in the subversion: the search for verbal precision resolves in inarticulate overwhelm. Deeply character-specific. Earns high scores because it works on multiple levels simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I scheduled all the meetings for March 31st because I genuinely believed the date didn't exist. I misremembered the rhyme. I thought it was 'Thirty days hath September, April, June, and November. All the rest have thirty-one, except February alone.' So March only has thirty days.

jokes.text: Jerry reveals he's been scheduling all meeting requests for March 31st because he didn't think March 31st existed, then sings the rhyme wrong.
jokes.setup: Leslie is confused why six people are waiting for meetings. Jerry proudly explains his system of scheduling everything for March 31st to avoid them.
jokes.punchline: His reason: 'Because I didn't think March 31st existed.' Then he sings the mnemonic rhyme incorrectly, including March among the 30-day months.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best premises. The absurdist internal logic is perfect — Jerry didn't maliciously avoid his job, he just used the wrong mnemonic. The singing of the rhyme with March incorrectly included is the cherry on top, showing Jerry's blissful ignorance extends to the very tool he used to make his mistake. Original, well-structured, completely Jerry-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, Humpty Dumpty had a great fall.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, it's 'Humpty Dumpty sat on a *wall*' — wait, no, that's right. But it's 'had a great fall,' not 'had a great fall.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I'm just — why are you teaching this to a child?

jokes.text: April tries to sing the '30 days has September' rhyme to verify March 31st exists and gets it wrong: '♪ 30 days has September, April, March, and November ♪'
jokes.setup: April is trying to recall the mnemonic rhyme to figure out how many days are in March
jokes.punchline: She misremembers it (putting March in the 30-day list instead of June), confirming she genuinely couldn't verify this
jokes.explanation: A brilliant callback and escalation of the previous joke. April didn't just lazily pick a fake date — she actually tried to verify it with the rhyme and botched the rhyme, getting March into the 30-day list. This deepens the character comedy: she failed twice. The misquotation is immediately corrected by Ron ('June and November'), making the structure crisp.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We had 93 meetings scheduled in a single day. I had to sit through all of them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Isn't it amazing? 93 meetings! That's a new record!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was a nightmare.

jokes.text: Leslie corrects Jerry: 'June and November.' Today is March 31st. 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Jerry sings the mnemonic with March included as a 30-day month.
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects him to 'June and November,' then confirms today is March 31st. Jerry's 'I know' lands as the punchline — he knows NOW, having just been corrected.
jokes.explanation: Jerry's 'I know' is perfectly timed deadpan — he knows now that she's corrected him, which makes it worse, not better. The economy is excellent; three words do a lot of work. Extends the previous joke rather than recycling it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to schedule even MORE meetings. But this time, I'm going to color-code them by priority AND emotional resonance. Plus, I'll add a ukulele performance between each one for morale.

jokes.text: Leslie asks how many meetings she has today. '93.' [Strangled groan]
jokes.setup: Leslie has been learning that Jerry scheduled everything for March 31st. She asks how many total meetings she has.
jokes.punchline: The answer is 93, followed by a strangled groan from Leslie.
jokes.explanation: The number 93 is funny in specificity — not 100, not 50, but exactly 93. The strangled groan is implied physical comedy. Functional but relies on the already-established premise's momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's a tragic historical story about a wedding that became a bloodbath.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: The only survivors were horses, not people.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'To me, this situation is a blood-soaked, nightmarish hellscape. However, to Leslie Knope... Oh, how fun. Yay.'
jokes.setup: Ron describes having 93 meetings in one day.
jokes.punchline: He articulates how horrifying it is to him, then pivots to a deadpan Leslie impression with maximum sarcasm: 'Oh, how fun. Yay.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The contrast between Ron's baroque horror ('blood-soaked, nightmarish hellscape') and his dismissive Leslie impression ('Oh, how fun. Yay.') captures both characters perfectly in a single beat. Could only be Ron. The phrase 'blood-soaked, nightmarish hellscape' for bureaucratic inconvenience is peak Swanson hyperbole and highly quotable. Earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I need you to listen to me very carefully. We need to coordinate the entire permit application process by end of business today.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm putting on my boots, just listen—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ow! Why are these so tight?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I almost have it—

jokes.text: Leslie suggests they try to get seven more meetings to make it an even 100. Ron tells her to stick to 93.
jokes.setup: They've just learned there are 93 meetings — already a catastrophe for Ron.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's instinct is to find MORE meetings to hit a round number, treating an emergency as an optimization problem.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Leslie-specific. Her compulsive over-achievement kicks in even when she's already drowning. Ron's weary 'just stick to 93' is the perfect straight-man cap. Great character integration — this is exactly what makes Leslie Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I brought you some coffee, Mark.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, thank you! You're so thoughtful.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hmm, this is... really not very good. Did you make this yourself? Because it tastes like you stirred it with a stick of butter.

jokes.text: Leslie takes her coffee and Ann's coffee for Mark, saying 'next time more sugar.'
jokes.setup: Ann arrives with coffee for Mark, not for Leslie. Leslie is rushing out and takes both coffees.
jokes.punchline: She drinks from Ann's coffee for Mark, then tells Ann 'next time more sugar' before disappearing.
jokes.explanation: Solid bit of oblivious Leslie energy — she takes someone else's gift and critiques it. The 'more sugar' note as she rushes off is the right comedic capper. Not exceptional but cleanly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need to get some concealer for this pimple that's about to form. Not just any concealer – it needs to be the right shade, the right texture, the right everything. Because when this pimple shows up, and it will show up, I need to be ready. Jessica cannot see me with a pimple. She cannot.

jokes.text: Jerry offers to 'set himself on fire and create a diversion' as an alternative to postponing the meetings.
jokes.setup: Ron asks what to do about the remaining meetings while Leslie is gone.
jokes.punchline: Jerry offers self-immolation as a practical solution, delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist beat. Jerry's willingness to harm himself to be useful is tragicomically on-brand. The word 'diversion' makes it sound procedural and tactical, which is the right comic register for this show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What cologne is that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called Intrude. The slogan is 'Intrude: Because she said no, but her pheromones said yes.'

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm gonna need more Ron Swansons.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs people to cover 93 meetings and has to find available staff.
jokes.punchline: She frames the solution as needing to clone or replicate the singular, inimitable Ron Swanson — as if that were a feasible resource.
jokes.explanation: Short and effective. The joke is that 'Ron Swansons' becomes a unit of measurement for manpower — which is absurd given how opposed Ron is to doing anything. Works on its own and gets better if you know the character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Alright, I'm taking this meeting thing seriously. I'm going deep undercover.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: From now on, I'm Special Agent Bert Macklin, FBI.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've got the badge, the suit, the whole thing. Nobody suspects a thing.

jokes.text: The Turnbill Mansion history: an interracial wedding ceremony was 'beautiful and romantic' — but then word got out and 'the reception was a bloodbath.'
jokes.setup: Bill describes a progressive 1867 wedding between a white woman and a Wamapoke Indian chief as beautiful and romantic.
jokes.punchline: Then word got out — 'and the reception was a bloodbath.'
jokes.explanation: The structure is nearly perfect: genuine pathos ('beautiful and romantic'), a pivot ('but then word got out'), and a brutally dry punchline ('bloodbath') that works both literally and as dark commentary on American racial history. 'Bloodbath' is the exact right word — clinical enough to be funny, honest enough to sting. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann, I want you to just sit there and don't say anything. Can you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think so.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Okay, we'll see.

jokes.text: 'Fortunately, there were two survivors. Unfortunately, they were both horses.'
jokes.setup: Bill has just described the reception as a 'bloodbath.' A natural follow-up is whether anyone survived.
jokes.punchline: There were two survivors — but they were both horses, making the 'fortunately' retroactively meaningless for any human.
jokes.explanation: The standout joke of the episode. The 'fortunately/unfortunately' construction is classically structured, and the pivot to horses is perfectly unexpected. 'Fortunately' raises hope; 'unfortunately' dashes it; 'they were both horses' is an absurdist punchline that recontextualizes the entire preceding sentence. Zero wasted words. Could be a standalone bit. Genuinely exceptional — earns the 8+ score comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, how old were you when I was in high school? Oh my God. Oh my God, that's weird. That's so weird.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: If we had a baby, and I had to babysit it while you were at work, I'd be like 60 years old.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'd be changing diapers with my walker. The baby would be like, 'Why is Grandpa here?' I'd be like, 'I'm your dad, sweetie.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And then I'd probably fall asleep during tummy time and the baby would crawl into the street.

jokes.text: Tom Haverford introduces himself to the historical society rep about 'former beauty queen Jessica wicks' and announces he'll be 'running point' on this.
jokes.setup: A serious historical preservation issue is being discussed. Leslie is appropriately concerned.
jokes.punchline: Tom completely ignores the preservation angle and essentially hijacks the meeting because there's an attractive woman involved.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom energy — his priorities are always wildly misaligned with the task at hand. 'Running point' is the right corporate-speak for him. Character-specific but not the freshest joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Nick Newport Sr.
dialogue.line: So you're the young man Leslie's been telling me about. Tell me, where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: I'm from Eagleton, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Nick Newport Sr.
dialogue.line: Eagleton? That's a fine town. Very... clean.

jokes.text: Leslie throws her boots at Tom to get his attention, says 'Oh, these are tight' when he complains.
jokes.setup: Leslie borrowed fur-lined boots from someone and needs Tom's attention urgently.
jokes.punchline: She throws the boot at Tom, and when he protests, she deflects by noting they were tight on her anyway.
jokes.explanation: Competent physical comedy beat with a serviceable topper. The boot detail is set up earlier (they're borrowed, they're tight) which gives it minimal payoff architecture, but the joke isn't remarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: She's a gold digger. And I'm attracted to gold diggers. So, gold digger digger.

jokes.text: 'Someone is trying to alter a gazebo.' — Leslie treating this as a genuine emergency requiring immediate departure.
jokes.setup: Ron points out they still have 91 meetings left and Leslie is abandoning them.
jokes.punchline: Leslie justifies it as an 'emergency': 'Someone is trying to alter a gazebo.' Delivered as if this were equivalent to a natural disaster.
jokes.explanation: Works because Leslie's priorities are hilariously specific and sincere. 'Alter a gazebo' is not the language of emergency, but she uses it with complete conviction. The joke is about bureaucratic passion misaligned with real-world stakes — quintessentially Parks and Rec.

jokes.text: Tom's cologne: 'Attack by Dennis Feinstein. When you want to attack the senses of the lady you want to bed.'
jokes.setup: Tom is preparing to meet Jessica wicks and sprays cologne in the car.
jokes.punchline: The cologne is called 'Attack' and its pitch is literally about attacking a woman's senses — Tom recites this as if it's a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Dennis Feinstein is a recurring absurdist character in the Parks universe, making his cologne names an ongoing bit. 'Attack' as a romantic fragrance is good absurdist naming. Tom's sincerity in reciting the tagline is perfectly oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: What's done is done.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's universal. I've never heard that in my life.

jokes.text: Everyone in the car reacts to Tom's cologne cloud — 'Door! Door! Door! Door! Close it.'
jokes.setup: Tom has applied his 'Attack' cologne liberally before getting in the car
jokes.punchline: Leslie and others in the car are overwhelmed and frantically demand the door be closed, presumably to trap the smell outside
jokes.explanation: A solid visual/physical comedy beat that pays off the cologne setup. The repetition of 'Door!' is funnier than a single word would be. Standard but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is why we need to preserve our history! We can't just tear down these buildings and forget where we come from!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's an absolute travesty, and I am... I am furious! So furious that I... I can't... What are those things? Those things that you see with?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Eyes?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! And those... those strips of the spectrum! The pretty ones!

jokes.text: Ron tells Ann she can 'head home early' and recruits her for meetings anyway, ending with 'Just sit there and don't ruin the city.'
jokes.setup: Ron is divvying up duties. He tells Ann he doesn't need her help, then immediately assigns her meetings.
jokes.punchline: 'Just sit there and don't ruin the city' — the lowest possible bar set for Ann's performance.
jokes.explanation: Peak Ron Swanson line. 'Don't ruin the city' as the literal job description is brilliant in its minimalism — it captures both Ron's contempt for government work and his low expectations for civilians. Highly quotable and completely character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I'd like to meet with Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron's dead. I'm his daughter.

jokes.text: Andy announces 'Bert Macklin, FBI, on the case' before taking meetings.
jokes.setup: Ron is assigning people to cover meetings and tells Andy he's in the conference room.
jokes.punchline: Andy responds by invoking his fictional alter ego 'Bert Macklin, FBI' as if this is a legitimate way to handle government meetings.
jokes.explanation: Bert Macklin is an iconic Andy character detail — his FBI alter ego that he slips into with complete sincerity. 'On the case' is the right register. High character integration because this is completely unique to Andy. Gets a rewatch bonus because fans know and love Bert Macklin.

dialogue.speaker: Ultimate Frisbee Representative
dialogue.line: We're here because we need funding for our league and—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You want me on your team? Yes! Oh my God, yes! I am so in!

dialogue.speaker: Ultimate Frisbee Representative
dialogue.line: No, we just need—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be so good at this. I'm gonna be the best ultimate frisbee player you've ever seen.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Can I get a badge?'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been assigned to cover official government meetings as an unqualified civilian.
jokes.punchline: His only concern is getting a badge — the surface-level trapping of authority, not the responsibility itself.
jokes.explanation: Three words of pure character. Andy's priorities are perfectly encapsulated: he doesn't care about the meetings, just about looking official. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not actually a parks employee. I'm a nurse.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. Can you look at this mole?

jokes.text: April's talking head about Andy: 'April is the best. But she's 20. When April was born, I was already in 3rd grade. Which means if we were friends back then, I'd have been hanging out with a baby. I don't know anything about infant care. My God, I could've killed her.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reflecting on his feelings for April and the age gap between them.
jokes.punchline: His logic spirals from age difference → hypothetical childhood friendship → infant danger → 'I could've killed her.' Each step is its own logical leap that somehow follows from the previous one.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The absurdist logic chain is perfectly calibrated to Andy's specific brand of dumb — he's not stupid, he just follows genuine reasoning to places no one else would go. 'I could've killed her' as the conclusion of a romantic reflection is inspired. The structure builds in escalating steps, each funnier than the last. Earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: This gazebo is just a mushy old pile of rot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, your husband is a mushy old pile of rot.

jokes.text: Jessica wicks mispronounces/mangles Leslie's name as 'Leslie Knorp.'
jokes.setup: Jessica greets Leslie warmly, claiming to remember her from judging the pageant together.
jokes.punchline: She gets Leslie's name wrong — 'Leslie Knorp.' Leslie's visible forced smile (implied) is the beat.
jokes.explanation: A well-worn comedic trope but executed cleanly. Establishes Jessica's character (she doesn't really remember or respect Leslie) efficiently. Not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not a stick in the mud! I love fun. I love parties. In fact, I'm going to throw the biggest party this town has ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But first, we need to shut down the current party because it's a safety hazard and someone could get hurt.

jokes.text: Nick Newport Sr. asks Tom: 'Tell me straight. Are you a Chinese?' Tom replies: 'No. I'm one of the Indian people.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been charming the Newports. Nick Sr. suddenly asks an abrupt, rude question about Tom's ethnicity.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response — 'one of the Indian people' — is both dignified and slightly absurdist in its formal phrasing, deflecting the rudeness with deadpan.
jokes.explanation: The joke does two things: characterizes Nick Sr. as a rich, oblivious, casually racist old man, and gives Tom a perfect deadpan response. 'One of the Indian people' has just enough formal distance to be funny — Tom is unflappable, and the phrasing is unexpected.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron is taking a bathroom break!

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'That floppy old bag of money is gonna be dead in, like, a month. And who's going to comfort Jessica and her millions of dollars? Yeah, Jessica's a gold digger, but I'm a gold digger digger.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just been charming the elderly Nick Newport Sr. while obviously focused on Jessica.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a gold digger digger' — Tom invents a new category for himself: someone who pursues gold diggers for their eventual windfall.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The concept of a 'gold digger digger' is genuinely original — it's a portmanteau of a plan wrapped in a wordplay escalation. Tom's willingness to share his mercenary strategy with total sincerity is peak character. The setup through the 'floppy old bag of money' framing makes the payoff land harder. Quotable, original, deeply Tom-specific. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Can you just give me a straight answer? Yes or no?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Beep boop beep! Whirrrr click click beep boop!

jokes.text: Jessica explains how she and Nick Sr. met: 'He was there because his blood doesn't work.'
jokes.setup: Jessica is telling a romantic origin story about meeting her husband at a hospital ribbon cutting.
jokes.punchline: 'His blood doesn't work' — a charmingly vague, accidentally hilarious explanation for a serious medical condition, delivered without any apparent awareness.
jokes.explanation: Five words that do enormous work. 'His blood doesn't work' is the kind of sentence a person says when they don't know (or don't care) what a medical condition actually is. It's the perfect Jessica line — beautiful, dim, and accidentally revealing about how little she knows or cares about her husband's health. Economy is near-perfect. Earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: When you're dealing with city bureaucracy, you have to be confident. You walk in there like you know exactly what you're doing, and they'll never question you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I have absolutely no idea what I'm talking about. I've never done this before in my life.

jokes.text: Jessica says 'where I come from there's a saying: what's done is done.' Leslie replies: 'That's a saying everywhere.' Jessica: 'I've never heard it before and I think it's a great saying.'
jokes.setup: Jessica uses a common saying as if it's a regional specialty.
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects her that it's universal. Jessica's response — she's never heard it and thinks it's great — reveals she genuinely doesn't know it's a common expression.
jokes.explanation: A three-beat joke that builds perfectly. The original claim is mildly odd; Leslie's correction is the straight-man pivot; Jessica's sincere approval of the 'new' saying she just discovered is the punchline. Characterizes Jessica as wealthy, insular, and oblivious without being cartoonish. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Is this swimsuit appropriate for the community pool?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not going to tell you how to live your life. But I will say this: that is not appropriate for my desk.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I should just pay you to follow me around.' Jessica: 'If that's a job offer, I accept.'
jokes.setup: Tom is flirting with Jessica after complimenting her appearance.
jokes.punchline: Jessica takes the throwaway flattery literally as a job offer and immediately accepts, suggesting she'd genuinely consider being paid to accompany Tom.
jokes.explanation: Cute but lightweight. The joke is in Jessica's literal reading of a figure of speech, which fits her character, but it's a fairly familiar comedic beat. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April started as a lowly squire, but she's risen through the ranks. She's now a knight in my department.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: However, like most knights, she's begun to question authority, burn down the castle, and attack her liege lord.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's me.

jokes.text: Tom to Jessica walking ahead of him: 'I should just pay you to follow me around.' Jessica: 'If that's a job offer, I accept.'
jokes.setup: Tom is complimenting Jessica's appearance from behind
jokes.punchline: Jessica misreads his flirtatious comment as a literal employment offer and accepts — inadvertently revealing she's interested in any money-related arrangement
jokes.explanation: A nice double joke — Tom's creepiness and Jessica's mercenary instincts collide. Works as character comedy for both.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, are you okay? Ron was really harsh back there.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm fine. Don't worry about it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, you can talk to me. That's what I'm here for.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, I don't need your sympathy. And I definitely don't need the camera's either.

jokes.text: Leslie, furious about the destruction: 'History is important. You just can't go around changing everything all the time or else next thing you know they'll be painting the white house... not white. I'm so angry I can't think of another color.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is outraged by the mansion alterations. She tries to make a dramatic point about changing historical things.
jokes.punchline: She gestures toward 'the White House' being painted a different color — then fails to name any other color because she's too angry to think.
jokes.explanation: Wonderful Leslie bit. The argument itself is already exaggerated (gazebo → White House), but the real joke is that she short-circuits mid-sentence because her anger has disabled her vocabulary. 'I'm so angry I can't think of another color' is a deeply human and funny admission of cognitive overload. The topper ('Green' from someone else) is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to end every interview with a signature catchphrase. Something like 'You just got Knoped!' Or 'That's a Knope from me!' Or 'Don't look a gift Knope in the mouth!'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That last one doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, neither does 'knocked up,' but people love it!

jokes.text: Citizen complaint: 'Your department banned me from attending games just because I yell "you suck" at the players.' Ron: 'According to the complaint, you yelled it at five-year-old girls.'
jokes.setup: A citizen frames his ban from park games as an unjust restriction on speech
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he was yelling 'you suck' at five-year-old girls' sports games
jokes.explanation: A sharp two-beat joke. The citizen frames himself as wronged; Ron's flat revelation of the truth ('you yelled it at five-year-old girls') is the perfect deadpan punchline. Economy is excellent — Ron delivers exactly the information needed, no more.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Son of a biscuit! Monkey fighting! Snakes on a plane!

jokes.text: April, impersonating Ron's daughter 'April Swanson,' tells the citizen that Ron is 'currently dead' and it's 'his last wish' that April have this meeting.
jokes.setup: April is covering Ron's meetings and the citizen asks for Ron Swanson.
jokes.punchline: April announces Ron is dead and this is his dying wish — completely fabricated, delivered with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly April. She commits fully to the bit — adopting a fake last name, inventing a death, and adding the 'last wish' detail for dramatic effect. Her deadpan delivery of complete nonsense is her defining comedic register, and this is one of the episode's best April moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I should have seen that coming.

jokes.text: April's meeting with the Frisbee league rep: she immediately joins the team, starts asking about jerseys and team name ('Are we the lightning?'), completely ignoring the actual meeting agenda.
jokes.setup: April is supposed to listen to a parks department request about scheduling conflicts.
jokes.punchline: Instead of taking notes or offering solutions, April declares 'You won me over. I will join your team.' and then escalates into logistics questions about jerseys and names.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation bit. April subverts the meeting format by treating it as a personal recruitment pitch she's enthusiastically accepting. 'Are we the lightning?' is a nice absurd detail. The rep's confused attempts to get back on track are implied.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know, I know, you're all thinking 'Here comes Tom with that bit again.' But I love this bit. I'm gonna do this bit forever.

jokes.text: Ann reveals to a citizen: 'I don't actually work in the parks department. I'm a nurse.' Citizen: 'That's great news. I have the weirdest thing on my arm.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been confessing she's not qualified for the meeting; the citizen is unsurprised
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots from park business to asking for free medical advice — 'I have the weirdest thing on my arm'
jokes.explanation: A tight setup-punchline. The citizen's pivot from civic complaint to free medical consultation is instantly relatable and perfectly timed. 'The weirdest thing on my arm' is just specific enough to be funny without overstaying.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Andy, you don't even work here anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know! And I'll quit again if you don't rehire April!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Your husband's a mushy, old, pile of rot.'
jokes.setup: Jessica says 'don't tell me about Pawnee history, the Newports made this town' and references her husband's 85th birthday.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, exasperated, retorts that Jessica's husband is 'a mushy, old, pile of rot' — an insult that mirrors the 'old, pile of rot' she'd used to describe the mansion.
jokes.explanation: A callback that lands harder because Leslie turns Jessica's dismissive language back on her husband. Leslie rarely insults people and the out-of-character directness is funny. The callback structure adds craft value.

dialogue.speaker: April's mom
dialogue.line: Oh Ron! Welcome, welcome! We're so excited to have you here!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Mom, please. You're embarrassing me.

dialogue.speaker: April's mom
dialogue.line: What? I'm just being friendly! Ron, can I get you anything? Coffee? Pie? I made three kinds!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: She made one kind. It's pumpkin.

jokes.text: Leslie calls Ron urgently. Ron's response: 'Leslie, I haven't relieved myself in five hours. So if you'll excuse me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is calling Ron with urgent gazebo news.
jokes.punchline: Ron's counter-argument for why he can't talk is that he hasn't urinated in five hours and he's prioritizing that over her emergency.
jokes.explanation: Ron's commitment to basic physical needs over bureaucratic nonsense is wonderfully character-consistent. '5 hours' is the right specific number — it implies he's been suffering through meetings. Deadpan delivery makes it funnier than the content alone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I didn't know you had a sister.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's my daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Leslie walks in on Councilman Howser using the bathroom. 'Miss Knope. Councilman Howser. Not that I saw anything other than your face.'
jokes.setup: Leslie bursts in urgently to discuss the gazebo with a nearby councilman.
jokes.punchline: She has clearly walked in on him in a compromising bathroom situation. Her immediate caveat — 'not that I saw anything other than your face' — signals she saw exactly that.
jokes.explanation: The clarification 'other than your face' is the punchline — she wouldn't need to say it if it were true. Classic cringe construction with good payoff timing. Leslie's mortified professionalism in the aftermath is implied.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Marriage is just a scam invented by the greeting card companies to make us buy more cards. Valentine's Day, anniversary cards, 'sorry I forgot our anniversary' cards...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then you start thinking about the wedding night, and it's beautiful, and romantic, and you're in a nice hotel...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But then a year later you're thinking about other weddings. Other wedding nights. You're imagining yourself at those weddings...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then you're not even invited to the weddings anymore, you're just outside the hotel window with binoculars.

jokes.text: After the bathroom encounter resolves, Leslie deadpans: 'I saw your penis.'
jokes.setup: The awkward Councilman Howser bathroom encounter has apparently concluded with some professional conversation.
jokes.punchline: As a parting shot or internal monologue, Leslie confirms: 'I saw your penis.' Stripping away all the euphemism she'd been using.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land enormously because of everything they're not saying. The contrast with her elaborate diplomatic phrasing ('not that I saw anything other than your face') makes the blunt callback hit harder. Perfect economy. One of the episode's most quotable beats.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know I'm the gate lady. I've accepted it. I've embraced it. I am the gate lady.

jokes.text: A citizen asks Andy to fix broken swings; Andy responds with a long constipated non-answer sound: 'Eeeeeee-boop!'
jokes.setup: Andy has been told by Ron not to say yes to anything. A citizen makes a completely reasonable request to fix one broken swing.
jokes.punchline: Andy is physically incapable of saying yes or no, so the pressure escapes as a nonsense sound: 'Eeeeeee-boop!'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely original physical comedy bit. Andy is caught between instruction and instinct, and the pressure finds an unexpected release valve. 'Eeeeeee-boop' is inspired — it's exactly what you'd sound like if your brain was trying to say both yes and no simultaneously. Deep character integration: Andy's people-pleasing instinct versus Ron's directive. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Have a good night, Duke Silver.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What did you just call me?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Duke Silver. Your secret jazz alter ego. I've known for like two years.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: How did you...

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have my sources. Also, you're not that good.

jokes.text: Mark and Ben have a thoughtful conversation about city gridlock and red tape — then Mark's talking head: 'I have no idea what I was saying.'
jokes.setup: Mark is shown apparently giving authoritative advice to Ben about navigating bureaucracy.
jokes.punchline: His talking head reveal: he had no idea what he was talking about and was just saying plausible-sounding bureaucracy words.
jokes.explanation: Good structural use of the mockumentary format — the talking head undercuts the authority projected in the prior scene. Mark's utter lack of self-consciousness about admitting this is funny. The joke is in how confident he sounded.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I can't make that time. Can we reschedule?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Sure. How about Octember 35th?

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: That's not a real date.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: How about Destroy-cember 42nd?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, those aren't real months.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine. Festivus at midnight o'clock.

jokes.text: A citizen asks Andy: 'Is this too revealing for a public pool?' while apparently placing their groin near Andy's desk. Andy: 'Kindly get your groin off my desk. So my body makes you uncomfortable too?'
jokes.setup: A citizen has come for a parks-related query about pool attire.
jokes.punchline: They are apparently demonstrating the swimwear in an extremely inappropriate way, and the citizen's follow-up ('my body makes you uncomfortable too?') implies this is a recurring rejection for them.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag inferred from dialogue. 'Kindly get your groin off my desk' is a perfect Andy line — he uses 'kindly' which adds a polite absurdity. The citizen's 'too?' reveals a history of rejection that deepens the comedy.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'April was supposed to be the moat that kept the citizen barbarians away from Swanson castle. Instead, she blew up the castle and stabbed me in the face.'
jokes.setup: April has made promises to citizens and created chaos instead of deflecting meetings.
jokes.punchline: Ron uses elaborate medieval metaphor to describe the situation — 'moat,' 'Swanson castle,' 'blew up the castle and stabbed me in the face.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top three jokes. The metaphor is so specifically Ron — medieval, self-aggrandizing ('Swanson castle'), and catastrophic. The escalation from 'moat' (defensive) to 'blew up the castle' (total destruction) to 'stabbed me in the face' (personal) is beautifully structured. The phrase 'Swanson castle' is intrinsically funny. This is character comedy at its finest — no other character in television could have said this. Easily earns 8.5+.

jokes.text: Ron to April: 'I don't care that you text all day and sleep at your desk. In fact, I encourage it. But only because you were doing that one thing... keeping this crap off my desk!'
jokes.setup: Ron is reprimanding April for screwing up. He begins by listing things she does that he apparently doesn't mind.
jokes.punchline: He has been actively endorsing her laziness because it came packaged with the one useful function: shielding him from work. The logic is completely inverted — he's not mad she was lazy, he's mad she stopped being useful while lazy.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Ron's management philosophy is entirely self-serving and anti-government — he literally built his office around an employee whose value was doing nothing. The structure is perfect: he appears to be listing grievances (texting, sleeping) but each one turns into a compliment, making the actual complaint land harder. Deeply Ron, deeply funny. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie addresses the reporter dramatically: '[dramatically] Gazebo? More like Ga-zoinks-Bo.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to get media attention for the gazebo situation and addresses a reporter with a recorder.
jokes.punchline: 'Ga-zoinks-Bo' is Leslie's attempt at a clever wordplay headline-grabber. The reporter immediately asks her to 'talk normally.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Leslie thinks this is a devastating rhetorical move. 'Ga-zoinks-Bo' is gloriously bad wordplay — it's not clever, which is the point. Her instinct to use a catchphrase in what she considers a media moment is very Leslie. The reporter's request to 'talk normally' is the right deadpan reaction.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'She may be a former beauty queen, but today she's the king of destroying history.' Reporter tells her to just talk normally. 'Okay, fine. Ga-zoinks-Bo.'
jokes.setup: The reporter has already asked Leslie to talk normally after the first 'Ga-zoinks-Bo'.
jokes.punchline: After a moment of appearing to comply, she repeats 'Ga-zoinks-Bo' as if this IS talking normally.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the previous joke. The callback lands because she literally does what was asked (she drops the dramatic delivery) but still says 'Ga-zoinks-Bo,' suggesting she genuinely thinks it's a coherent phrase. Leslie's commitment to the bit is character-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Sweetums owns the Pawnee journal.' Leslie: 'Crrr-AP on the cob.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to get media coverage of the gazebo story but learns the local paper is owned by the very family destroying it.
jokes.punchline: 'Crrr-AP on the cob' is Leslie's G-rated expletive for the situation — a uniquely folksy, all-ages expression of total dismay.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable and Leslie-specific lines. 'Crap on the cob' is a uniquely Midwestern, government-employee-who-can't-swear-at-work expression. The elongated 'Crrr-AP' delivery is implied and adds a layer of repressed intensity. Could only come from Leslie Knope. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: The reporter reveals there's one more meeting — with them, and it's about them quitting. 'I quit.'
jokes.setup: Leslie thinks the meeting with the reporter is the last item on her media advocacy agenda.
jokes.punchline: The reporter announces the meeting is actually about their own resignation — delivered with maximum dramatic timing.
jokes.explanation: A fun structural twist — the 'meeting' pivot is unexpected. The timing of 'I quit' as a punchline is clean. Not exceptional but well-constructed misdirection.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Thank God! That was it, right?' Reporter: 'Uh, no, there's one more.' Leslie: 'Damn it to hell!' Reporter: 'It's with me. And it's right now. And it's about me quitting.'
jokes.setup: Leslie thinks the bad news (Sweetums owns the paper) is the last surprise
jokes.punchline: There's one more meeting — with the reporter himself, who proceeds to quit on the spot
jokes.explanation: The 93-meetings premise pays off in an unexpected way — one of the meetings is with a person who intends to quit during it. 'Damn it to hell' as Leslie's exact reaction to there being one more thing is perfectly calibrated. The beat structure (relief → false hope → worse news) is well-executed.

jokes.text: Leslie chains herself to the gazebo gate; tells Tom to 'throw away the key. Seriously?' 'Yes, throw it!' — Tom throws the key
jokes.setup: The demolition crew is arriving to tear down the gazebo; Leslie has chained herself to the gate
jokes.punchline: She instructs Tom to throw away the key — Tom does it despite clear misgivings — taking the civil disobedience to its logical extreme
jokes.explanation: Leslie's escalating civil disobedience is funny through commitment. Tom's 'seriously?' pause before actually throwing the key shows his disbelief that this is happening.

jokes.text: Leslie chains herself to the gate to stop demolition equipment. Tom: 'Really thought that gate would open in the middle.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has chained herself to the mansion gate to stop a demolition vehicle.
jokes.punchline: The gate does not open in the middle — it presumably opens to the side, dragging Leslie with it. Tom's observation is perfectly useless.
jokes.explanation: Tom's observation is the perfect bystander comment — the joke is not the physical comedy itself but his casual, completely unhelpful post-mortem. 'Really thought that gate would open in the middle' suggests he had formed a theory that has now been disproven. Funny in its specificity and nonchalance.

jokes.text: Leslie talking-head: 'I really thought that gate would open in the middle.'
jokes.setup: The mechanized gate has apparently closed on Leslie while she was chained to it, or she was dragged with it
jokes.punchline: Her post-incident reflection is not regret about chaining herself to a gate, but disappointment that the gate didn't open symmetrically
jokes.explanation: Leslie's post-incident analysis focuses entirely on the gate's engineering rather than the obvious problem of chaining yourself to it. Her complaint is specific ('I thought it would open in the middle') suggesting she had planned around a different gate configuration. Perfect Leslie logic applied to a catastrophic situation.

jokes.text: Tom keeps snapping the gate (the mechanism) after the gazebo is destroyed. 'Cut it out, Tom.' 'It never gets old!'
jokes.setup: The gazebo has been destroyed and Leslie is upset.
jokes.punchline: Tom is gleefully snapping the gate back and forth, delighted by the mechanism, completely oblivious to the emotional weight of the moment.
jokes.explanation: Tom's childlike delight in the gate mechanism against Leslie's devastation is solid tonal comedy. 'It never gets old!' is perfectly Tom — he's found something new and shiny. Good character contrast.

jokes.text: Leslie's gate injury explanation: 'Nothing's bruised but my ego and my arm a little from the mechanized gate.'
jokes.setup: Ann and Mark ask if Leslie is okay after the gate incident.
jokes.punchline: 'Nothing's bruised but my ego and my arm a little' — the 'and my arm a little' undercuts the noble self-deprecation of 'just my ego.'
jokes.explanation: The cliché 'nothing bruised but my ego' is subverted by the addendum — she IS physically hurt, she just buries it in the grammar. Classic Leslie: perform stoicism, accidentally reveal vulnerability.

jokes.text: Andy to Ron: 'Either you hire her back or I quit.' Ron: 'You don't work for me.' Andy: 'And I never will, sir. Good day.'
jokes.setup: Andy is passionately advocating for April to be re-hired by Ron.
jokes.punchline: He issues an ultimatum — then Ron points out Andy doesn't work for him, making the resignation threat meaningless. Andy doubles down: 'And I never will, sir. Good day.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Andy's ultimatum is already sweet and impulsive. Ron's correction is perfect deflation. But the real payoff is Andy's refusal to back down despite having been logically cornered — 'And I never will, sir. Good day.' The 'sir' and 'good day' are the key details, turning it into an absurd act of principled defiance that means nothing. Earns the 8+ easily.

jokes.text: April's mom calls her 'Zuzu' and her father calls Ron 'Zuzu's boss.' April's parents treat Ron like a guest, Ron is visibly uncomfortable.
jokes.setup: Ron shows up at April's house to rehire her. He meets her very warm, normal, domestic parents.
jokes.punchline: April's parents call her 'Zuzu' — a babyish nickname that completely undercuts April's carefully constructed gloomy persona. Ron's discomfort in a warm, domestic setting is implied.
jokes.explanation: The entire premise — April has a warm, loving, completely normal family — is a perfect character reveal. 'Zuzu' is the ideal nickname because it's so at odds with April's aesthetic. Ron's discomfort in domestic warmth adds a second comedy layer. Gets a rewatch bonus because it enriches understanding of April's character.

jokes.text: 'Welcome to Castle Ludgate!' — April's mom greeting Ron with theatrical enthusiasm.
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at a normal suburban house.
jokes.punchline: April's mom greets him like he's arrived at a mansion: 'Welcome to Castle Ludgate!' — with genuine, oblivious pride in a regular house.
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy for the Ludgate parents (warm, cheerful, totally unself-aware) and as an indirect joke about April — she lives in 'Castle Ludgate.' The callback to earlier's 'Swanson castle' is a nice unintentional echo.

jokes.text: Ron encounters April's sister and says 'You must be April's sister. I'm Ron.' Then a long pause and [clears throat] 'Nice to meet you.'
jokes.setup: Ron is navigating the Ludgate home and encounters April's sister.
jokes.punchline: The prolonged pause before 'Nice to meet you' implies April's sister is extremely attractive and Ron had to compose himself. The cleared throat is the tell.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in the pause. Ron is visibly affected in a way he would never admit. [Clears throat] before 'Nice to meet you' is doing enormous work — Ron performing normalcy while clearly blindsided. A purely visual/physical comedy beat inferred from the transcript with perfect economy.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head about Mark and Ann: 'It was supposed to be me and Ann, or me and Jessica, or Ann and Jessica with me watching.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reacting to the news that Ann and Mark might be getting married.
jokes.punchline: He lists his own romantic scenarios, which escalate from understandable (me and Ann) to delusional (me and Jessica) to something else entirely ('Ann and Jessica with me watching').
jokes.explanation: An escalating three-part list that builds to an unexpected place. The structure is pitch-perfect: each item is more outrageous than the last, and the final item recontextualizes the whole list. Tom's sincerity makes it funnier — he's not embarrassed. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie's reason for being upset isn't the gazebo — it's that 'every time a couple gets married, I'm about to lose two good friends.'
jokes.setup: Tom tells Leslie that the gazebo wasn't entirely what she was upset about. She admits it.
jokes.punchline: Her concern is losing Ann and Mark as friends once they marry — framed with Leslie's characteristically literal social math.
jokes.explanation: More emotional than comedic, but the framing ('I'm about to lose two good friends') is Leslie's particular brand of earnest social accounting. Gets a moderate score because it's warm and real but not primarily a joke.

jokes.text: Leslie crashes the Newport birthday party to give a toast. 'I know you're probably thinking there's that crazy gate lady from outside back again.'
jokes.setup: Leslie walks into a private birthday party uninvited.
jokes.punchline: She immediately identifies herself as 'the gate lady,' acknowledging how others see her, before pivoting to her actual purpose.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-awareness that she is 'the gate lady' to these people is funny because she doesn't seem embarrassed by it — she just states it as a known fact, then proceeds anyway. Good character moment.

jokes.text: Leslie's toast escalates: 'to change, and forgiveness, and the future, and Ann and mark, and happiness, and Nick Newport, Sr. May all your future gazebos live long and prosper.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to give a gracious, conciliatory toast at the Newport party.
jokes.punchline: The toast keeps expanding to include more and more people and concepts, culminating in the absurd 'May all your future gazebos live long and prosper' — which is both a Star Trek reference and a complete non sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of who/what Leslie is toasting is classic Leslie — she can't stop adding things. The payoff 'May all your future gazebos live long and prosper' is inspired because it both apologizes for the gazebo and wishes more gazebos upon them, which is either generous or a veiled threat. The 'live long and prosper' phrasing adds absurdist register.

jokes.text: 'Please leave.' 'Is it weird if I ask to take a piece of cake with me? I won't. Go.'
jokes.setup: Jessica has had enough of Leslie and tells her to leave.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's impulse is to ask for cake — she starts to ask, then talks herself out of it mid-sentence — before Jessica cuts her off anyway.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to leave without at least asking about the cake is great character comedy. The speed of her self-correction ('I won't. Go.') before Jessica can answer — pre-empting her own rejection — shows Leslie's conflict between desire and social awareness.

jokes.text: Ron tells April he wants her to come back. April: 'Well, I don't want to come back. The end.' Ron: 'I was talking to Andy about you. And he made me realize I need you back.' April: 'What did he say?' Ron: 'Don't recall.'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to persuade April to return to work. He credits Andy with changing his mind.
jokes.punchline: When April asks what Andy said, Ron admits he 'doesn't recall' — meaning either Andy's argument was so stupid it's already gone, or Ron just wanted to invoke Andy's name without repeating the sentiment.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly calibrated Ron moment. He's admitting Andy moved him while simultaneously refusing to give Andy (or anyone) the dignity of remembering what they said. 'Don't recall' is the ideal Ron response — clipped, unyielding, and somehow both dismissive and tender. The fact that April immediately agrees after this non-answer is the real payoff. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: April reveals she knew Ron was 'Duke Silver' the entire time: 'Bye, Duke Silver. My mom has all your albums. I recognized you the day we met.'
jokes.setup: Ron (as Duke Silver, his secret jazz musician alter ego) has just been busted by April's mom.
jokes.punchline: April reveals she's known all along — since day one. Ron's carefully maintained secret was never a secret to April.
jokes.explanation: A landmark Parks and Rec moment. The Duke Silver reveal to April recontextualizes the entire Ron/April relationship — she's had this leverage since day one and never used it. Ron's response ('Good girl') is the perfect cap: he's not embarrassed, he's impressed. This is character comedy at its best — it works perfectly both for first-time viewers and gets better on rewatch. Earns high scores for character integration and structure.

jokes.text: April's farewell: 'Bye, Zuzu. Bye, Duke Silver.' — said to Ron in front of her family
jokes.setup: April is leaving with Ron; she says goodbye to her family
jokes.punchline: She casually calls Ron 'Duke Silver' as she leaves — also acknowledging his secret identity, like her mother did
jokes.explanation: April calling Ron 'Duke Silver' as she leaves is a warm callback — establishing that she too knows his secret. Ron's non-reaction is the punchline.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Good girl.' — after April reveals she's kept Duke Silver secret.
jokes.setup: April has just revealed she's known Ron is Duke Silver all along and never told anyone.
jokes.punchline: 'Good girl' — Ron's highest form of praise, delivered with complete seriousness. Two words conveying deep respect in Ron's emotional register.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect economy. In Ron's emotional vocabulary, 'Good girl' is profound approval — he almost never expresses anything positive directly. The joke is that this tiny, dry acknowledgment is enormous coming from him. Inseparable from the preceding reveal but distinct as a beat. Maximum economy score.

jokes.text: A citizen returns the next day trying to reschedule their meeting with Ron. April's new scheduling: 'June 50th,' '2:65,' 'March-tember one-teenth.'
jokes.setup: A citizen missed their meeting and wants to reschedule.
jokes.punchline: April offers a series of completely fabricated dates — 'June 50th,' '2:65,' 'March-tember one-teenth' — each more absurd than the last, deliberately recreating Jerry's original scheduling error but with full knowledge.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional closing callback that pays off the episode's central premise. April has absorbed the lesson of Jerry's mistake and weaponized it — she's now intentionally creating impossible dates to deflect meetings. 'March-tember one-teenth' is the peak of the joke: three made-up words combining two months. The escalation across three fake dates (each more absurd) is perfectly structured. One of the episode's best jokes. Earns 8+ comfortably.

tmdb_overview: Ron is furious when April mistakenly schedules a ton of meetings for him. Meanwhile, Leslie fights to preserve a historical landmark.
insight: Forty-one jokes in 24 minutes lands below Parks' season average despite strong character-driven cringe work.
